patient.chief_complaint: Progressive proximal leg weakness and difficulty rising from chairs over 4 months
patient.history_present_illness: A 72-year-old former smoker with treated non-small cell lung cancer in remission (squamous cell, stage II, surgery + adjuvant chemotherapy 3 years ago) presented for evaluation of progressive proximal leg weakness over 4 months. He initially noticed difficulty rising from low chairs and climbing stairs approximately 4 months ago. He attributed this to deconditioning after his cancer treatment. Over 2 months, the weakness progressed to difficulty rising from the toilet without the safety rail and climbing stairs required use of the handrail. He denies ptosis or diplopia. His wife reports his voice becomes slightly slurred after dinner conversations lasting more than 20 minutes. He has also had increasing dryness of the mouth over the past 6 months, which he attributed to his medication side effects. He mentioned to his urologist that he had developed erectile dysfunction approximately 6 months ago. He does not have significant sensory symptoms in his hands but notices mild numbness and tingling in his feet. His deep tendon reflexes were noted to be diminished at a recent appointment. He underwent surveillance CT chest 6 weeks ago for his lung cancer remission — reported as no evidence of disease recurrence. He was initially referred to physical therapy for 'deconditioning' without improvement. Oncology attributed his weakness to chemotherapy-related peripheral neuropathy and added B12 supplementation. He was subsequently referred to neurology when a repeat EMG performed by his oncologist showed unexpected findings suggesting possible NMJ involvement in addition to mild sensorimotor neuropathy.

specialized_test.impression: 1. Low baseline CMAP amplitudes (deltoid 0.8 mV, median 1.2 mV; reference >3-4 mV). High-rate RNS (50 Hz) demonstrates pathological CMAP increment of 142% in deltoid and 128% in trapezius (threshold >100%). Post-exercise facilitation confirmed in deltoid (0.8 mV to 2.0 mV after 10-second MVC). These findings indicate a pre-synaptic disorder of neuromuscular transmission (low baseline CMAP with high-rate and post-exercise facilitation), in contrast to a post-synaptic pattern. 2. Mildly reduced SNAP amplitudes bilaterally (sural 4 µV) — mild axonal sensorimotor neuropathy. Anti-VGCC antibody testing and paraneoplastic panel recommended

results.title: LEMS: distinguishing paraneoplastic from autoimmune
results.finding: 60-70% of LEMS is paraneoplastic (SCLC most common); anti-SOX1 positive in 65% of SCLC-LEMS vs <5% of autoimmune LEMS; anti-VGCC positive in >90% of LEMS regardless of etiology; LEMS can precede SCLC detection by 2 years

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS), paraneoplastic, secondary to new small cell lung cancer (SCLC); anti-VGCC P/Q-type positive, anti-SOX1 positive

differential.key_features: MG can produce fatigable weakness but typically shows decrement (not increment) on RNS and normal baseline CMAP; here baseline CMAP low with >100% facilitation at 50 Hz and AChR negative.
Inflammatory myopathy raises CK and shows myopathic EMG; here CK normal and RNS facilitation is diagnostic of pre-synaptic NMJ disorder.
Could explain mild reduced SNAPs but does not produce >100% facilitation on RNS or proximal weakness improving with brief exercise.
Botulism is acute, descending, with autonomic features and bulbar involvement; this is sub-acute over months without an exposure.
Patient is anticoagulated but not on a statin; CK normal.

optimal_actions.action: Order anti-VGCC P/Q-type and N-type antibodies, anti-SOX1, plus standard AChR and MuSK to exclude MG
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Anti-VGCC P/Q positive (LEMS); anti-SOX1 positive (paraneoplastic SCLC marker); AChR/MuSK negative

optimal_actions.action: Order RNS with high-rate (20-50 Hz) post-exercise facilitation protocol
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Low baseline CMAP with >100% increment after brief MVC or 50 Hz RNS confirms pre-synaptic LEMS

optimal_actions.action: CT chest with contrast for occult SCLC (most common LEMS-associated malignancy)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: May be negative initially — SCLC can be small; PET-CT recommended if standard CT non-diagnostic

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hypermetabolic hilar/lung lesion supports occult SCLC; guides biopsy

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-contributory for neuromuscular junction disorders.
CSF has no diagnostic role in LEMS or MG.
Brain MRI is non-contributory for LEMS unless an alternative CNS cause is being entertained.

sequence_constraints.reason: Confirm anti-VGCC/SOX1 serology before initiating LEMS-specific symptomatic therapy or oncologic referral.

critical_actions: RNS with high-rate facilitation protocol — low baseline CMAP with >100% increment is diagnostic
CT chest + PET-CT to search for occult SCLC (LEMS often precedes radiographic tumor by months)
Oncology referral for staging and treatment of underlying malignancy
Initiate symptomatic therapy with amifampridine (3,4-DAP) after ECG and drug-interaction review
Plan repeat surveillance imaging at 3-6 month intervals for up to 2 years if initial PET-CT negative
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT diagnose this as myasthenia gravis based on fatigable weakness alone — RNS facilitation pattern and anti-VGCC positivity place this in the LEMS category.
Do NOT prescribe aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, or NMBs — these worsen any pre-synaptic NMJ disorder.
Do NOT delay oncologic workup once anti-VGCC + anti-SOX1 positive — paraneoplastic LEMS frequently precedes detectable SCLC.
key_reasoning_points: LEMS is the principal MG mimic the case is designed to test — pre-synaptic NMJ failure with low baseline CMAP and high-rate facilitation is the discriminator.
Anti-VGCC P/Q-type antibody is positive in 85-90% of LEMS; anti-SOX1 raises paraneoplastic concern for SCLC.
Smoker with prior NSCLC: standard CT may miss small SCLC; PET-CT is essential.
Patient improves with brief exercise (post-activation facilitation) — the opposite pattern to MG; this clinical sign is highly specific.
Treat the underlying SCLC and use amifampridine for symptomatic control; IVIG and immunosuppression are second-line.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude that 'NMJ disease excluded' and miss LEMS.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: AChR-negative does NOT exclude pre-synaptic NMJ disorders; anti-VGCC is the discriminating test for LEMS.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Standard CT has limited sensitivity for small lung primaries; LEMS often precedes radiographic SCLC by months — PET-CT is required and surveillance continues for up to 2 years.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: AFib does not produce fatigable proximal weakness or RNS facilitation; the underlying pathology is paraneoplastic LEMS.
